name: Leigh Syndrome with Cardiomyopathy

criteria.description: Progressive neurological deterioration with psychomotor regression
Bilateral symmetric lesions in basal ganglia and/or brainstem on MRI
Evidence of mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme deficiency or elevated lactate in blood/CSF
Clinical or imaging evidence of cardiomyopathy (e.g., hypertrophic or dilated) associated with Leigh syndrome
Identification of pathogenic variants in mitochondrial or nuclear genes associated with Leigh syndrome

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of progressive neurological deterioration with characteristic bilateral brain lesions on MRI and biochemical evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Cardiomyopathy presence supports diagnosis but is not mandatory; genetic testing aids confirmation.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Bilateral symmetric necrotic lesions in basal ganglia and brainstem
searchTerms: dead tissue spots in brain movement centers
damage in basal ganglia and brainstem areas
heart muscle disease with thickening or dilation

common.symptomName: Elevated blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate levels
searchTerms: high lactic acid in blood and spinal fluid
elevated lactate levels in body fluids
eye movement problems like shaking or paralysis
abnormal eye motions such as nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia

rare.notes: Rarely reported in Leigh syndrome with cardiomyopathy

laboratory: Elevated lactate and pyruvate levels in blood and CSF
imaging: Bilateral symmetric lesions in basal ganglia and brainstem on MRI
Cardiac MRI or echocardiogram showing hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy
genetic: Pathogenic variants in mitochondrial DNA genes (e.g., MT-ATP6)
Nuclear gene mutations affecting mitochondrial function (e.g., SURF1, NDUFS4)
other: Muscle biopsy showing ragged-red fibers or mitochondrial abnormalities

distinguishingFeatures: Stroke-like episodes with focal neurological deficits
Onset typically later in childhood or adolescence
Onset before age 20 with pigmentary retinopathy
Cardiac conduction defects rather than cardiomyopathy

redFlags: Rapidly progressive neurological decline in infancy or early childhood
Bilateral symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions on MRI
Evidence of cardiomyopathy in a child with neurological symptoms
references: Finsterer J. Leigh and Leigh-like syndrome in children and adults. Pediatr Neurol. 2008.
Lake NJ, et al. Leigh syndrome: One disorder, more than 75 monogenic causes. Ann Neurol. 2016.
Rahman S, et al. Diagnosis and management of Leigh syndrome: a consensus statement from the Mitochondrial Medicine Society. Genet Med. 2017.
